description: Misspelled words (not intentional dialect or character voice).
Missing, incorrect, or inconsistent punctuation.
examples: Apostrophes in contractions: "hadnt" → "hadn't", "wasnt" → "wasn't"
Apostrophe confusion: "it's tail" (wrong) vs "its tail" (possessive)
Missing comma after introductory clauses: "When she arrived she sat" needs comma after "arrived"
Unclosed or mismatched quotation marks in dialogue
Missing Oxford comma in a list of three or more items: "apples, oranges and pears" → "apples, oranges, and pears"
notes: Serial/Oxford comma: only flag when there are THREE OR MORE items in a list and the comma before the final conjunction is absent. Do NOT flag two-item constructions ("dubstep and death metal" is correct as-is). Do NOT flag a sentence where the Oxford comma is already present. Do NOT flag compound predicates ("she overdosed and disappeared" is not a list). Do NOT flag noun phrases joined by 'and' that form a pair rather than a series.

description: Two or more consecutive spaces between words where only one is expected.
examples: "She  walked" or "the  door" → flag the extra space

description: Use of "--" (double hyphen) where an em dash "—" should be used in fiction prose.
examples: "He paused--unsure" → should be "He paused—unsure"
notes: Flag every occurrence of "--" in the excerpt.

description: A content word (noun, verb, adjective, or adverb) used 2 or more times within a single paragraph or 5 consecutive sentences. Exclude: articles (a, an, the), prepositions, conjunctions, pronouns (she, he, they, her, his, it), and auxiliary verbs (is, was, were, had, have, has, will, would, could, should, may, might, must, shall, do, did, been, be).
examples: "She walked to the door. He walked past. She walked back." → "walked" ×3 → flag it
notes: Only flag full lexical verbs (e.g. walked, said, looked), nouns, adjectives, and adverbs — not auxiliaries or function words.

description: Incorrect preposition use — the wrong preposition attached to a verb or adjective.
examples: "arrived to" → "arrived at"
"interested on" → "interested in"
"capable to" → "capable of"
"married with" → "married to"
"afraid from" → "afraid of"
"insist to" → "insist on"
notes: Focus only on clear preposition errors. Do not flag stylistic choices or dialect.

description: Missing hyphen in a compound modifier used directly before a noun (attributive position).
examples: "a well known investigator" → "a well-known investigator"
"a last minute decision" → "a last-minute decision"
"a long established practice" → "a long-established practice"
notes: Only flag when the compound modifier precedes the noun. Do NOT flag when it follows a linking verb — "the author is well known" is correct without a hyphen.

description: In fiction prose, cardinal numbers one through nine should be spelled out as words. Flag numerals in that range used where words are expected.
examples: "She had 3 cats" → "three cats"
"7 people arrived" → "seven people"
"There were 2 options" → "two options"
notes: Do not flag: numbers 10 and above, years (1987), times with a.m./p.m. (6 a.m.), measurements with unit abbreviations, or numbers used as labels/identifiers.

description: An adjective or adverb that adds no meaning and should be deleted. Common offenders: very, really, quite, rather, somewhat, actually, basically, literally, just, simply, a bit.
examples: "She was very tired" → "She was tired" (or find a stronger adjective: "exhausted")
"He literally ran" → "He ran"
"She was actually surprised" → "She was surprised"
"It was quite cold" → "It was cold"
notes: Only flag when removing the word changes nothing. Do not flag modifiers that genuinely establish degree, contrast, or tone — and do not flag in dialogue where the word may authentically reflect a character's speech.

description: An unnecessary "that" following a reporting or cognitive verb (said, told, knew, thought, felt, believed, noticed, found, realised, understood, etc.) where it can be removed without any change in meaning or clarity.
examples: "She said that she was leaving" → "She said she was leaving"
"He knew that the door was locked" → "He knew the door was locked"
"She noticed that his hands were shaking" → "She noticed his hands were shaking"
notes: Do not flag "that" used as a relative pronoun ("the book that she read"), a demonstrative ("that was the problem"), or in any case where removal would create ambiguity or awkwardness.

description: A generic verb, often propped up by an adverb, where a single precise verb would be stronger. Common offenders: walked + adverb, said + adverb, looked at, got up, went into, moved + adverb.
examples: "She walked slowly to the door" → "She shuffled to the door"
"He said quietly" → "He murmured"
"She went into the room" → "She entered the room"
"He looked at her carefully" → "He studied her"
notes: Flag only clear cases where a verb-plus-adverb construction has a single, obviously stronger replacement. Do not flag every common verb — only where the pairing is conspicuously weak and a better word is unambiguous.

description: A multi-word construction that can be replaced by a single word or short phrase without loss of meaning.
examples: "in the event that" → "if"
"due to the fact that" → "because"
"at this point in time" → "now"
"in spite of the fact that" → "although"
"was able to" → "could"
"in order to" → "to"
"on account of" → "because"
notes: Flag only established wordy constructions. Do not flag longer phrasing used deliberately for rhythm, emphasis, or a character's voice.

description: An imprecise word in narration where something more specific would strengthen the prose. Common offenders in narration: thing, stuff, nice, got, good, bad, big, small, a lot, somehow, something.
examples: "She picked up the thing from the table" → name what it is
"It was a nice afternoon" → describe what made it nice
"He got the letter" → "He found" / "retrieved" / "received" the letter
"Somehow she knew" → specify the sensation or reasoning
notes: Flag only in narration, where the author controls word choice. Do not flag in dialogue, where vague language may authentically reflect the speaker's voice or education.

description: Three or more consecutive sentences that open with the same grammatical structure, creating a monotonous rhythm in the prose.
examples: "She opened the door. She walked inside. She sat down." → three consecutive sentences with identical subject-verb opening
"The light faded. The room grew cold. The fire died." → three short declaratives with identical noun-verb structure
notes: Flag only when three or more consecutive sentences share the same opening pattern. Do not flag intentional anaphora used for deliberate rhetorical or emotional effect.

description: A word so rare, technical, archaic, or domain-specific (including clinical, psychological, or scientific jargon used outside its professional context) that it is likely to halt a general fiction reader, and where a common synonym or plain phrase exists and would serve equally well.
examples: "Her expression was adamantine" → "Her expression was unyielding"
"He moved with oleaginous ease" → "He moved with an oily, ingratiating ease"
"The room had a minatory stillness" → "The room had a threatening stillness"
"She kept perseverating on the argument" → "She kept dwelling on the argument"
"His affect was blunted" → "His emotions seemed dulled"
"The treatment was iatrogenic" → "The treatment itself caused the harm"
notes: Flag words that are genuinely obscure to a general reader — not merely formal or elevated. This includes clinical and psychological terms (e.g., 'perseverating', 'hypervigilant' used as unexplained jargon, 'affect' in the psychiatric sense) when used in narrative prose without contextual clarification. Do NOT flag: intentional stylistic voice or register; period-appropriate vocabulary in historical fiction; specialist terms that are contextually defined or necessary (e.g., a medical thriller where the POV character is a doctor explaining their field); words that are elevated or literary but widely recognizable (e.g., 'melancholy', 'ephemeral', 'acrid'). The test is whether a typical adult fiction reader would need to stop and look the word up.

description: A verb or phrase that unnecessarily filters action through the POV character's perception, creating distance between the reader and the story. Common offenders: saw (that), heard, felt, noticed (that), realised/realized (that), watched, observed, sensed.
examples: "She saw that the door was open" → "The door was open"
"He heard the clock strike" → "The clock struck"
"She noticed that the room was cold" → "The room was cold"
"She felt the floor was uneven" → "The floor was uneven"
notes: Flag in close third-person or first-person narration where removing the filter still preserves the POV anchor. Do not flag where the filter is itself the point — e.g., "She heard something she couldn't identify" (the uncertainty is meaningful). Do not flag every use of these verbs, only where a direct construction is clearly better.

description: A sentence that winds up without delivering, using an empty introductory frame before the actual content. Common patterns: "It was [X] that...", "What [subject] [verb] was...", "The thing about [noun] was...", "There was something about..."
examples: "It was then that she realised the door was open" → "She realised the door was open"
"What struck her was how quiet it had become" → "How quiet it had become" or restructure
"There was something about his manner that unsettled her" → "His manner unsettled her"
"It was only when she reached the end that she saw" → "Only when she reached the end did she see"
notes: Flag only when the entire introductory frame can be cut and the sentence still delivers its full content. Do not flag expletive constructions used deliberately for rhythm, emphasis, or to build suspense.

description: A passive construction where the agent is known or clearly present in the sentence, and an active verb would be stronger or clearer.
examples: "The letter was left on the desk by him" → "He left the letter on the desk"
"She was handed the envelope by the courier" → "The courier handed her the envelope"
"The files had been moved by someone" → "Someone had moved the files"
notes: Flag only when the agent appears in the sentence (e.g., "by the clerk") AND active construction is unambiguously better. Do not flag: passives where the agent is intentionally withheld for mystery or suspense, idiomatic passives ("He was born in Vienna", "The meeting was adjourned"), or constructions where the passive is standard ("She was given the news").

description: An emotion named directly as a label in narration, where showing through physical sensation, action, or behaviour would be more effective in fiction.
examples: "She felt nervous" → show dry mouth, racing pulse, inability to sit still
"He was angry" → show clenched jaw, clipped speech, sharp movements
"She felt relieved" → show exhaled breath, loosened posture, sudden quiet in the chest
"She was frightened" → show held breath, cold hands, reluctance to move
notes: Flag clear, single-word or short-phrase emotion labels in narration: felt sad, was angry, felt nervous, felt relieved, was frightened, felt happy, felt guilty, felt embarrassed, was excited. Do not flag: in dialogue, where characters name their feelings naturally; or where a character analytically reflects on their own state over an extended passage rather than simply labelling it.

description: A character name, place name, or other proper noun appears with two different spellings within the same excerpt, OR a proper noun is spelled consistently but in a way that deviates from its conventional real-world spelling, suggesting either a continuity error or an unintentional misspelling the author should confirm. This includes cases where a name is spelled the same way throughout but unconventionally (e.g., 'Abbot' where 'Abbott' is standard), which may be intentional but warrants a flag for author confirmation.
examples: "Hartmann" in one sentence, "Hartman" two sentences later
"Mireille" then "Mireil" in the same passage
"Rennick" becoming "Renwick" mid-paragraph
"Jack Abbot" used consistently, but the conventional spelling of this surname is "Abbott" — flag for author to confirm if intentional
"Katarine" used throughout where "Katharine" or "Catherine" are conventional — flag as possible misspelling
notes: Only flag spelling inconsistencies when both spellings appear within the current excerpt. Additionally, flag proper nouns that are spelled consistently but unconventionally compared to their standard real-world form, noting that the deviation may be intentional and asking the author to confirm. Do NOT flag: (1) genuine nicknames or aliases that are clearly intentional (e.g., a character introduced as 'Thomas, or Tom, as everyone called him'); (2) cases where one form is clearly a dialogue quotation of how another character mispronounces the name; (3) invented fantasy or sci-fi names with no conventional real-world spelling to compare against, unless two different spellings appear in the same excerpt. When flagging an unconventional-but-consistent spelling, phrase the flag as a confirmation request rather than a definitive error.
